notices.title: General information, not legal advice
notices.text: OpenReady offers educational project guidance. License selection, compatibility, ownership, and third-party material may require qualified legal advice.

notices.title: Planning guidance, not a security assessment
notices.text: A policy, threat model, test, or high score does not prove that software is secure. Verify risks against the project's real architecture and operating environment.

notices.title: Guidance, not accessibility certification
notices.text: Automated checks and templates do not establish WCAG conformance. Record actual human testing, known barriers, and supported environments honestly.

license.whyItMatters: A clear license tells people what they may use, copy, modify, and distribute. A public repository without a license does not automatically grant those permissions.
minimum: Place a recognized open-source license in the repository root.
Name the license in the README.
Confirm the copyright holder and year are accurate.
stronger: Review whether code, documentation, screenshots, and other assets are covered.
Record required third-party notices and incompatible material.
Review contribution licensing before accepting substantial outside work.
commonMistakes: Assuming a public repository is automatically open source.
Using custom restrictions that conflict with open-source use.
Copying images or code without checking their terms.
exampleEvidence: A root-level LICENSE file.
A README license section linking to the license.
A third-party notices file when attribution is required.

code-of-conduct.whyItMatters: A Code of Conduct makes participation expectations visible and gives the community a shared standard for responding to harmful behavior.
minimum: Publish behavior expectations in a top-level file.
Explain where the policy applies.
Provide a private reporting route and describe possible consequences.
stronger: Add conflict-safe handling when the normal recipient is involved.
Set acknowledgement and confidentiality expectations.
Document anti-retaliation and reconsideration safeguards.
commonMistakes: Publishing a policy without an enforcement process.
Using only a public issue for sensitive reports.
Naming an independent contact who has not agreed to serve.
exampleEvidence: CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md linked from the README.
A private reporting address or platform form.
Documented enforcement levels and conflict handling.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Code of Conduct

readme.whyItMatters: The README is usually the first place a user or contributor decides whether the project is understandable, useful, and active.
minimum: Explain what the software does and who it helps.
Provide basic use or installation instructions.
Link the license, contribution guide, security policy, and community channels.
stronger: Add screenshots or examples that match the current release.
State project scope and non-goals.
Include release status, support expectations, and accessibility information.
commonMistakes: Leading with internal history instead of the user problem.
Leaving setup steps incomplete or outdated.
Claiming features, scores, or compliance that have not been verified.
exampleEvidence: A README with purpose, use, contribution, support, and license sections.
A current interface screenshot with useful alternative text.
Links to releases, roadmap, issues, and discussions.

contributing.whyItMatters: Clear contribution instructions reduce uncertainty and help people participate through code, documentation, testing, accessibility, design, and issue reporting.
minimum: Explain how to report an issue and propose a change.
Provide local setup and verification steps.
Describe the expected pull-request scope and review process.
stronger: Offer first-contribution pathways and suitable labels.
Recognize non-code work explicitly.
Explain role progression, conflicts of interest, and sensitive-report routes.
commonMistakes: Assuming contributors already know the toolchain.
Requiring large changes for a first contribution.
Leaving response and review expectations undefined.
exampleEvidence: CONTRIBUTING.md with setup and testing steps.
Good-first-issue and help-wanted examples.
A pull-request template with accessibility and security checks.

changelog.whyItMatters: A changelog helps users and contributors understand notable behavior changes, compatibility risks, and release history.
minimum: Keep an Unreleased section.
Record meaningful additions, changes, fixes, accessibility work, and security work.
Date released versions consistently.
stronger: Link release entries to GitHub Releases or tags.
Separate current evidence from historical audit results.
Document migrations and compatibility expectations.
commonMistakes: Listing every commit without explaining user impact.
Editing old release facts to match the current version.
Presenting planned work as already released.
exampleEvidence: CHANGELOG.md with dated release sections.
Links to release notes and migration guidance.
Clear Unreleased entries for merged but unpublished work.

roadmap.whyItMatters: A public roadmap explains project direction while helping maintainers distinguish priorities from promises.
minimum: List current and planned work.
Link planned work to issues where possible.
Mark shipped, deferred, and cancelled work honestly.
stronger: Define release gates and acceptance criteria.
Invite focused community feedback on significant changes.
Keep the roadmap aligned with the current public application.
commonMistakes: Using dates as guarantees without capacity.
Keeping completed work marked as planned.
Adding broad ideas without owners, scope, or verification.
exampleEvidence: roadmap.md with current release goals.
A parent roadmap issue with child implementation issues.
Release gates covering tests, documentation, and deployment.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Leadership and Governance

issues.whyItMatters: A welcoming issue tracker gives users a clear route to report problems, suggest focused improvements, and find contribution opportunities.
minimum: Provide issue templates or clear reporting prompts.
Use descriptive labels and respectful triage.
Explain where sensitive security or conduct reports belong.
stronger: Maintain good-first-issue and help-wanted work.
Acknowledge valid reports within a realistic window.
Explain closures, deferrals, duplicates, and out-of-scope decisions.
commonMistakes: Sending sensitive reports to public issues.
Leaving stale issues without status context.
Treating every request as an implementation promise.
exampleEvidence: Bug, accessibility, and feature issue forms.
Labels for documentation, accessibility, security, and beginner work.
Maintainer comments explaining triage decisions.

security.whyItMatters: A security policy tells reporters how to share sensitive concerns without creating avoidable public harm.
minimum: Identify supported versions.
Provide a private reporting channel.
Request reproduction, impact, and environment details without asking for secrets.
stronger: Define acknowledgement, severity, remediation, and coordinated-disclosure expectations.
Link a threat model and incident-response process.
Explain project-specific in-scope and out-of-scope examples.
commonMistakes: Using a public issue for exploit details.
Promising fixed response times that maintainers cannot meet.
Treating the presence of SECURITY.md as proof the software is secure.
exampleEvidence: SECURITY.md with private reporting instructions.
GitHub private vulnerability reporting when enabled.
A documented severity and disclosure process.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Security Best Practices

governance.whyItMatters: Governance makes authority, decisions, permissions, and continuity understandable to contributors and users.
minimum: Name the current maintainers.
Explain how routine and significant decisions are made.
Describe maintainer responsibilities.
stronger: Define contributor and maintainer role progression.
Document conflict handling, inactivity, temporary absence, and succession.
Explain project transfer, archival, and emergency authority.
commonMistakes: Claiming community governance when one person makes every decision.
Granting repository access without criteria.
Ignoring what happens when the sole maintainer is unavailable.
exampleEvidence: GOVERNANCE.md with roles and decision classes.
Public discussion for significant changes.
Least-privilege permission and succession criteria.

resources.label: Open Source Guides: Leadership and Governance

community-docs.whyItMatters: A project site should help people understand and participate in the software rather than function as unrelated promotional content.
minimum: Link source code, license, releases, issues, and contribution guidance.
Keep site content directly related to the software and community.
Keep project status and version information accurate.
stronger: Publish accessibility, security, governance, and support documentation.
Show current development activity and roadmap evidence.
Keep hosting attribution and project purpose visible.
commonMistakes: Adding unrelated commercial or promotional sections.
Leaving the website behind the repository release.
Using community language without participation routes.
exampleEvidence: A software-focused public site with repository links.
Release history and roadmap pages.
Visible community policies and contribution routes.
